reference.source: Standard nephrology and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal dominant disorders causing slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with a bland urinary sediment and little or no proteinuria
The commonest subtypes are caused by variants in UMOD (uromodulin) and MUC1 (mucin-1); other genes include HNF1B, REN and SEC61A1
The UMOD form is classically associated with early-onset hyperuricaemia and gout, sometimes preceding renal impairment
Imaging and urinalysis are typically unremarkable, so a strong family history of unexplained CKD across generations is often the key clue
Kidneys may be normal or small with occasional medullary cysts; overt cysts are inconstant, so absence does not exclude the diagnosis
Progression to kidney failure usually occurs over decades, with wide variability even within the same family
Definitive diagnosis relies on genetic testing, as histology shows nonspecific tubulointerstitial fibrosis; MUC1 variants may need specialised assays
reference.pathophysiology: ADTKD is a family of monogenic tubulointerstitial diseases in which a defective protein disrupts tubular epithelial cell function and triggers progressive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. In the UMOD form, mutant uromodulin misfolds and is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum of thick ascending limb cells, causing cellular stress, impaired sodium handling that promotes urate retention (hyperuricaemia and gout), and eventual nephron loss. In the MUC1 form, a frameshift variant generates an abnormal mucin-1 protein that accumulates and injures tubular cells. Regardless of gene, the shared final pathway is chronic tubulointerstitial injury with fibrosis, producing slowly declining glomerular filtration with characteristically bland urine and minimal proteinuria.
additionalDifferentials: Reflux nephropathy and chronic obstructive uropathy
Analgesic or other chronic interstitial nephritis
additionalInvestigations: Serum urate, especially seeking early-onset or disproportionate hyperuricaemia
Urinalysis and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating bland sediment and low-grade proteinuria
Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and any medullary cysts
Detailed multigenerational family history and eGFR trajectory
Targeted genetic testing (UMOD, MUC1, HNF1B, REN) with specialised MUC1 assays where standard sequencing is negative
Kidney biopsy in selected cases showing nonspecific tubulointerstitial fibrosis
redFlags: Rapidly declining renal function inconsistent with the usual indolent course
Anaemia disproportionate to CKD stage, suggesting the REN subtype
Recurrent or tophaceous gout at a young age
Progression to advanced CKD requiring planning for renal replacement or transplantation
reference.prognosis: The disease progresses slowly, typically over several decades, culminating in kidney failure at a variable age even within families; the extrarenal burden is limited, and kidney transplantation is not complicated by disease recurrence in the graft.
pitfalls: Dismissing the diagnosis because imaging and urinalysis look normal
Missing the diagnosis when standard gene panels fail to detect the MUC1 variant
Attributing early gout solely to lifestyle rather than considering UMOD disease
Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and failing to screen at-risk relatives
